openingProblem.problem: In 1989 Poland was insolvent and ruled by a discredited Communist Party. By 1999 it was a NATO member with Europe's fastest-growing economy of the late 1990s, yet in 1993 and 1995 voters returned former Communists to power. Was Poland's transition a success?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: success, failure, or something in between?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: 1989: from Round Table to Solidarity government
chunks.body:
By the late 1980s Poland's Communist government had run out of options. Inflation had averaged over 50 per cent a year through the decade, and the foreign debt kept growing. In November 1987 the regime held a referendum on economic reform; a Solidarity-inspired boycott kept turnout down to 67 per cent and the referendum failed, the government's first defeat at the polls. Strikes paralysed the country in the spring and autumn of 1988, and in the autumn the whole government resigned.

The way out was negotiation. **Round Table** talks between the government and Solidarity opened in February 1989. In April they agreed that Solidarity would be legal, that a presidency would be created, that the Catholic Church would receive full legal status, and that a new Senate would be freely elected, with part of the lower house, the Sejm, also opened to direct election. The regime expected these semi-free elections to preserve its majority.

The elections of June 1989 destroyed that hope. Solidarity won 99 of the 100 Senate seats. Voters also crossed out the names of unopposed government candidates, so many failed to win the 50 per cent they needed. The new parliament named General Jaruzelski president by the slenderest of margins, but the Communists could no longer govern alone. Wałęsa chose not to lead the government himself and put forward Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a Catholic intellectual, who became the first non-Communist prime minister in the Soviet bloc in late summer 1989.

Mazowiecki's government still contained Communists in key ministries, and Jaruzelski remained head of state. Poland's revolution was negotiated, gradual and legal, a continuation of the "self-limiting" strategy of 1980–81. This mattered because the Communists surrendered power through institutions they had designed, which meant that Poland's new democracy began with a working parliament and without bloodshed, but also with members of the old regime still in place.

Within a year the transition accelerated. Jaruzelski resigned in September 1990, opening the way for a presidential election. By then the new government had already launched the most radical economic reform in the former Soviet bloc.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Economic crisis forced the regime to negotiate with Solidarity.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Gorbachev's refusal to back force also mattered, as the collapse section shows.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Round Table produced a negotiated, legal transfer of power.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The regime designed the elections to keep a majority; Solidarity's sweep was not part of the bargain.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The transition kept members of the old regime in place.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Their presence eased the transition and avoided confrontation.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Poland's transition began as a negotiation because the Communist regime could no longer govern alone.
useItInAnEssay.prove: After strikes paralysed the country in 1988, Round Table talks in February–April 1989 legalised Solidarity and created a freely elected Senate, of which Solidarity won 99 of 100 seats in June.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the Communists lost power through institutions they had designed themselves, so the change was legal and peaceful.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Jaruzelski became president and Communists kept key ministries, so the old regime remained partly in place.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Poland's start was therefore a negotiated compromise that ensured a peaceful transition at the price of continuity.

chunks.title: Shock therapy: the Balcerowicz Plan
chunks.body:
Poland's new government inherited an economy that was, in Judt's words, "insolvent in all but name". Its finance minister, **Leszek Balcerowicz**, chose the "big bang": a one-time, overnight switch to a market economy rather than a gradual reform. Judt explains his reasoning. Poland could not recover without international aid, and aid would come only if Poland built structures that reassured Western lenders. By anticipating the demands of the International Monetary Fund rather than waiting for them, Poland would earn the help it needed. And it had to move fast, "during the post-Communist honeymoon and before people realized how painful the process would be".

On **1 January 1990** the programme began. The government built up foreign reserves, removed price controls, tightened credit and cut subsidies, which meant allowing loss-making enterprises to fail. Real wages immediately fell by about 40 per cent. Unlike the failed reforms of the 1970s, the plan openly accepted unemployment, with a fund to support and retrain the jobless. What had changed, Judt notes, was the political climate: a government with popular legitimacy could impose pain that the Communists could not.

The short-term cost was severe. GDP fell by 31.5 per cent between 1990 and 1992, and consumer prices rose almost sixfold. But the economy recovered quickly. Growth reached just under 7 per cent in 1995 and 5.5 per cent in 1996 and 1997, and by 1997 Poland was attracting large foreign investment and growing faster than any other economy in Europe. Most growth came from new private firms: the private sector's share of GDP rose from 50 per cent in 1992 to about 70 per cent in 1997.

Privatisation of big state enterprises was slower. Three years after the revolution only 16 per cent of state-owned businesses had been sold, and much early privatisation, Judt observes, simply legalised the black market or sold the viable parts of state firms to local entrepreneurs with foreign money. This mattered because Poland's growth came mainly from new businesses rather than from selling old ones, which meant that Poland avoided much of the insider plunder seen in Russia, but kept many unproductive state industries.

The costs fell unevenly. By the end of the century agriculture produced only 3 per cent of GDP but employed a fifth of the workforce, and pensioners and laid-off workers saw little benefit. These losers of reform would shape Polish politics in the 1990s.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Shock therapy worked in Poland in the medium term: a sharp fall was followed by Europe's fastest growth.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The fall was very deep: GDP down 31.5 per cent and real wages down 40 per cent.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Speed was a political choice, made while the new government still had popular support.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The pain later fuelled the return of the ex-Communists in 1993.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Growth came from new private firms more than privatisation of old ones.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Slow privatisation left inefficient state industries in place.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Shock therapy succeeded in Poland in the medium term, though at a heavy short-term cost.
useItInAnEssay.prove: From 1 January 1990 Balcerowicz removed price controls and cut subsidies; real wages fell about 40 per cent and GDP fell 31.5 per cent by 1992, but growth reached just under 7 per cent in 1995.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a painful collapse cleared the way for new private firms, so the private sector's share of GDP rose from 50 to about 70 per cent by 1997.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the costs fell on farmers, pensioners and the unemployed, and in 1993 voters returned the former Communists.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Shock therapy was therefore an economic success but a political risk, judged by growth rather than by who paid.

chunks.title: Politics of transition: Wałęsa, fragmentation and the ex-Communists
chunks.body:
Once Communism was gone, the unity of the opposition dissolved. After Jaruzelski resigned in September 1990, Lech Wałęsa challenged his own former ally, Mazowiecki, for the presidency and won in December 1990. According to John Radzilowski in the *Encyclopedia of Modern Europe*, this split the Solidarity movement and led to a series of short-lived governments, while Wałęsa extended the power of the presidency and stretched its constitutional limits.

Party politics fragmented. In the parliamentary election of October 1991, 69 parties competed and 29 won seats, none with more than 14 per cent of the vote. The result was weak coalitions without clear mandates: Poland had five prime ministers and four governments between 1991 and 1993. Large-scale privatisation, the restructuring of giant Soviet-era industries and a new constitution were all hard to achieve.

Then the former Communists returned. In the September 1993 election the most popular parties were the Polish Peasant Party and the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), both largely made up of ex-Communists or figures from past governments. The Worldmark Encyclopedia of Nations notes three interpretations of the result: a rejection of shock therapy, nostalgia for the more ordered life of the past, and a vote against the Catholic Church's attempt to control social questions such as abortion, the school curriculum and women's role.

Fears that they would reverse the transition proved unfounded. The government of the Peasant Party leader Waldemar Pawlak and his SLD partner stayed committed to democracy and economic reform, differing mainly on its pace. In the 1995 presidential election the SLD leader, **Aleksander Kwaśniewski**, beat Wałęsa by 51.7 per cent to 48.3 per cent. By then, Radzilowski writes, Wałęsa "had lost the support of most of his fellow Poles"; when he ran again in 2000 he won 1 per cent.

How should this be judged? The return of the ex-Communists could look like failure. But a peaceful change of government through elections, with the losers accepting the result and the winners keeping the reforms, is a sign that democracy works. This mattered because power passed back and forth between Solidarity's heirs and the former Communists without either side abandoning democracy or the market, which meant that Poland's transition survived the unpopularity of its own reforms.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The break-up of Solidarity's unity after 1990 produced fragmented, unstable governments.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Fragmentation reflected real differences in the electorate once the common enemy was gone.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The ex-Communists' victory in 1993 was a protest against the costs of shock therapy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was also a vote against the Church's social agenda, not only economics.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Alternation in power showed democracy was working.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Rising unemployment and the rise of Lepper's Self-Defence suggest discontent remained.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the reasons why the former Communists won the Polish elections of 1993.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The former Communists won in 1993 mainly because many voters blamed shock therapy for their hardship.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Real wages had fallen about 40 per cent and GDP 31.5 per cent in 1990–92, and the Worldmark Encyclopedia of Nations notes that the result was read as a rejection of shock therapy and nostalgia for a more ordered life.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the losers of reform, such as pensioners, farmers and the unemployed, turned to parties promising a gentler pace of change.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the vote was also against the Church's social agenda and the chaos of fragmented governments, so economics was not the only reason.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Economic pain was therefore the main reason, but the ex-Communists won by promising to manage reform, not to reverse it.

chunks.title: Poland by 2000: success or disappointment?
chunks.body:
By the late 1990s Poland had settled the shape of its new state. A new **constitution** passed the National Assembly in April 1997 and was approved by referendum on 23 May 1997. In the parliamentary elections of 1997 the heirs of Solidarity returned: Solidarity Electoral Action and the Freedom Union formed a coalition under Jerzy Buzek, which reorganised local government, replacing 49 provinces with 16 in 1999. Kwaśniewski, a reformed Communist, was re-elected president in 2000. Power changed hands peacefully, by election, between left and right.

Abroad, Poland turned firmly west. In 1997 NATO invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to join, and they became members in **March 1999**, a decade after Poland had been a member of the Warsaw Pact. Judt places Poland in the "first tier" of post-Communist states which, after "a slough of economic despond" in the early 1990s, re-emerged "on a more secure foundation, able to attract Western investors and envisage an eventual ascent into the European Union".

But the decade ended with problems. Growth slowed after the Russian financial crisis of 1998, to 4 per cent by 2000, and unemployment rose from 13 per cent in 1999 to 15 per cent in 2000. Agriculture remained a weak point, producing only 3 per cent of GDP but employing a fifth of the workforce. Judt notes that for millions of pensioners, laid-off workers and peasants the transition was "at best an ambiguous benefit". Their discontent found new outlets at the end of the 1990s in farmers' and "popular" parties such as Andrzej Lepper's Self-Defence, which blended nationalism with regret for the old order.

So was Poland's transition a success? Measured against its starting point, an insolvent state with a discredited ruling party, the record is strong: a working democracy with regular changes of government, a market economy that grew faster than any other in Europe by 1997, membership of NATO, and a realistic path to the European Union. Measured by who gained and who lost, the picture is mixed. Radzilowski's judgement on Wałęsa's presidency could stand for the decade: Poland established "the rule of law", restored "a market economy" and began "rejoining the community of Western nations", but at the price of a divided political movement and a society in which the costs were unevenly shared. This mattered because Poland became the model of a successful transition, which meant that its problems with unemployment and rural poverty were often overlooked.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Politically, Poland's transition succeeded: a new constitution and peaceful alternation in power.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Fragmentation in 1991–93 showed how fragile the early system was.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Internationally, Poland moved decisively west: NATO in 1999 and a path to the EU.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: EU membership came only in 2004, outside this period.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Socially, the transition had clear losers: unemployment, farmers and pensioners.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Growth by 1997 was the fastest in Europe, so many Poles also gained.

To what extent was shock therapy a success in Poland between 1990 and 1997?

useItInAnEssay.claim: By 2000 Poland's transition was a political success with unresolved social costs.
useItInAnEssay.prove: A new constitution was approved by referendum in May 1997, power changed hands by election in 1993, 1995 and 1997, and Poland joined NATO in March 1999.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that democracy and a Western orientation were secure, so the core aims of 1989 had been achieved.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, unemployment rose to 15 per cent in 2000, and Judt notes that for pensioners, laid-off workers and farmers the change was at best an ambiguous benefit.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Poland's transition was therefore successful judged by its institutions, but incomplete judged by who shared its gains.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was shock therapy a success in Poland between 1990 and 1997?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far shock therapy succeeded, and by which measure

modelPlan.thesis: Shock therapy largely succeeded by 1997, turning a deep fall into Europe's fastest growth through new private firms; but its costs fell on farmers, pensioners and the unemployed, and voters punished its authors in 1993.

arguments.claim: The big bang: prices freed, subsidies cut (named factor first).
Deep fall, then fast growth driven by new private firms.
Slow privatisation of big state enterprises.
Social and political costs: the 1993 election.

modelPlan.counter: The costs were so high that voters rejected the reformers in 1993, so the policy's political price was severe.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judged by growth and private enterprise by 1997, it succeeded; judged by who paid, it was much more mixed.

segments.text: Shock therapy largely succeeded in Poland by 1997, though at a heavy initial cost.
From 1 January 1990 Balcerowicz freed prices and cut subsidies; GDP fell 31.5 per cent by 1992, yet growth reached just under 7 per cent in 1995.
This meant that the collapse of unviable state firms cleared space for new private businesses, which made up about 70 per cent of GDP by 1997.
However, real wages fell about 40 per cent, and in 1993 voters returned the ex-Communists, partly as a rejection of shock therapy.
Shock therapy was therefore an economic success but a social burden, and its success should be judged by its medium-term results.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The return of the former Communists to power showed that Poland's transition had failed.” Discuss with reference to the period 1989 to 1995.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far 1993 showed failure, or the opposite

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely wrong: 1993 showed that voters were unhappy with the costs of reform, but the ex-Communists kept democracy and the market, so their return demonstrated that the transition was working.

arguments.claim: For: the vote rejected shock therapy and expressed nostalgia.
For: fragmentation and five prime ministers in 1991–93.
Against: the ex-Communists kept democracy and reform.
Against: power changed hands peacefully again in 1995.

modelPlan.counter: Lepper's populists later showed discontent was deep, so 1993 was an early warning.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did democracy and the market survive the 1993 government? Yes, so the transition did not fail.

segments.text: The return of the former Communists in 1993 showed discontent with the costs of reform, not the failure of the transition.
The SLD and the Peasant Party won in September 1993, but their government stayed committed to democratisation and economic transition.
This meant that voters could punish the reformers without overturning the reforms, which is how a working democracy behaves.
However, the vote did reflect a rejection of shock therapy and nostalgia for a more ordered life, so many Poles felt the transition had failed them.
The claim is therefore largely invalid: 1993 showed the transition's costs, but also its strength.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the successes and failures of Poland's transition to democracy between 1989 and 2000.

decodeKey.judgement: Which outweighed the other, by a stated criterion

modelPlan.thesis: The successes outweighed the failures: Poland built a working democracy with a new constitution, peaceful changes of government and NATO membership; its failures lay in fragmented early governments and the uneven social costs of reform.

arguments.claim: Success: a negotiated, peaceful transfer of power.
Success: constitution (1997), alternation in power, NATO (1999).
Failure: fragmentation and five prime ministers in 1991–93.
Failure: unemployment, rural poverty and populist protest.

modelPlan.counter: The rise of Lepper's Self-Defence and 15 per cent unemployment suggest that many Poles did not see success.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judged by whether democratic institutions survived painful reform, the transition succeeded.

segments.text: Poland's transition to democracy succeeded, because its institutions survived the unpopularity of its own reforms.
Power passed peacefully to the ex-Communists in 1993, to Kwaśniewski in 1995 and back to Solidarity's heirs in 1997, and a new constitution was approved in May 1997.
This meant that losers of reform could change the government by vote, so no group had reason to abandon democracy.
However, unemployment reached 15 per cent in 2000, and populist parties such as Lepper's Self-Defence drew wide support.
The successes therefore outweighed the failures, though the failures shaped the politics of the next decade.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the roles of Wałęsa and Kwaśniewski in Polish politics between 1990 and 2000.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The roles of Wałęsa and Kwaśniewski

modelPlan.thesis: Both presidents kept Poland on a democratic, market and Western course, but they came from opposite camps and played opposite roles: Wałęsa, the Solidarity hero, divided his own movement, while Kwaśniewski, the ex-Communist, reassured voters that the old left had accepted democracy.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both kept democracy and the market.
Similarity: both served as elected presidents and faced fragmented parliaments.
Difference: Wałęsa split Solidarity and stretched presidential power.
Difference: Kwaśniewski won twice and saw the constitution through.

modelPlan.counter: Their roles reflected circumstances more than personality: Wałęsa faced the hardest years of reform, Kwaśniewski the years of recovery.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most for Polish democracy? Kwaśniewski's acceptance of the system, which showed it could absorb the old regime's heirs.

segments.text: Wałęsa and Kwaśniewski both kept Poland on a democratic course, but from opposite camps.
Wałęsa, elected in December 1990, split Solidarity and stretched the powers of the presidency, whereas Kwaśniewski, who beat him by 51.7 to 48.3 per cent in 1995, was re-elected in 2000.
This meant that the hero of 1980 divided the movement that had defeated Communism, while the ex-Communist reassured voters that the old left now accepted democracy.
However, during Wałęsa's presidency reforms established the rule of law and a market economy, so his record was not only one of division.
The decisive difference was therefore that Kwaśniewski's success showed Polish democracy could absorb the heirs of the old regime.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons why the former Communists won the Polish elections of 1993.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship

modelPlan.thesis: The ex-Communists won mainly because voters blamed shock therapy for their hardship; the chaos of fragmented governments and a reaction against the Church's social agenda added to their appeal.

arguments.claim: The costs of shock therapy.
Fragmentation and unstable governments.
Reaction against the Church's social agenda.
The split in Solidarity under Wałęsa.

modelPlan.counter: Growth was already returning by 1993–94, so economics alone does not explain the vote.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason, if removed, would most have changed the result? The costs of shock therapy, since they created the voters the ex-Communists won.

segments.text: The former Communists won in 1993 mainly because many voters blamed shock therapy for their hardship.
Real wages had fallen about 40 per cent and GDP 31.5 per cent in 1990–92, and the Worldmark Encyclopedia of Nations reads the vote as a rejection of shock therapy.
This meant that pensioners, farmers and the unemployed turned to parties promising a gentler pace of change.
However, the vote was also a reaction to five prime ministers in two years and to the Church's social agenda, so it was not purely economic.
The costs of reform were therefore the main reason, with political chaos and the Church question reinforcing them.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the impact of economic transformation on Polish society between 1990 and 2000.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Economic transformation divided Polish society: it created a new private sector and growth, but left pensioners, farmers and the unemployed behind, and their discontent shaped politics through the decade.

arguments.claim: Immediate shock: wages and output fell.
New private firms and foreign investment.
Losers: farmers, pensioners and the unemployed.
Political reaction: 1993 and populism.

modelPlan.counter: Strong growth from 1994 meant many Poles gained, so the losers were a minority.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which impact lasted longest? The division between winners and losers, which shaped politics through the decade.

segments.text: Economic transformation divided Polish society into clear winners and losers.
By 1997 new private firms produced about 70 per cent of GDP, yet by 2000 agriculture still employed a fifth of the workforce while producing 3 per cent of GDP, and unemployment reached 15 per cent.
This meant that the young, urban and entrepreneurial gained, while farmers and the jobless were left behind, so discontent persisted despite growth.
However, by 1997 Poland had the fastest growth in Europe and attracted large foreign investment, so the gains were widespread.
The deepest impact was therefore the division between winners and losers, which explains both the 1993 vote and the rise of Lepper's populists.
